Scenario 1: Business Logic Update 
Scenario: A company’s auto insurance division needs to update the threshold for automatically 
approving windshield repair claims from $200 to $300. The business managers want to make 
this change themselves frequently without waiting for the IT development team to release a 
new application version. 
Question: Which Pega modularity feature allows the development team to empower business 
managers to make this change? 
Options: 
Rule Versioning 
Rule Delegation 
Rule Reuse 
Situational Layer Cake 
Explanation: Delegation specifically allows business users to update dynamic business rules 
(like thresholds or decision tables) independently, without altering the core application code.

Scenario 2: Fixing a Broken UI 
Scenario: A junior developer is modifying a "Customer Contact" UI form (which is a Rule) in an 
application. They accidentally delete a critical email field and save the changes. The team needs 
to restore the form to exactly how it was yesterday without affecting any other part of the 
active Case processing. 
Question: Which feature provides the ability to undo this specific change safely? 
Options: 
Create a new Rule Type 
App Studio background generation 
Rule Versioning 
Relevant Records 
Explanation: Pega maintains a history of changes for every individual Rule. Versioning allows you 
to review the history and revert (undo) changes to that specific Rule without breaking the rest 
of the application.

Scenario 3: Rule vs. Rule Type 
Scenario: You are tasked with creating a new automated decision process that routes a 
customer's loan application based on their credit score. You select a Decision Table template to 
build this logic. 
Question: In Pega terminology, what is the Decision Table template, and what is the specific 

credit score logic you just built? 
Options: 
The template is a Rule; the logic is a Rule Type. 
Both the template and the logic are Rule Types. 
The template is a Rule Type; the logic is a Rule. 
Both the template and the logic are Rules. 
Explanation: A Rule Type is the abstract template (like the concept of a Decision Table). The 
Rule is the actual, specific instance you created (the credit score routing logic) which defines 
the behavior for your application.

Scenario 1: Versioning Choice 
Scenario: Users report that when they click the "Submit" button on a travel request, a typo in 
the confirmation message says "Thank you for your odrer" instead of "order". The development 
team needs to deploy a fix. 
Question: Which Ruleset version update is most appropriate for this change? 
Options: 
Patch version 
Minor version 
Major version 
Base version 
Explanation: A typo is a defect/bug. Bugs are always fixed using a Patch version update (e.g., 
moving from 01-01-01 to 01-01-02).

Scenario 2: Naming Conventions 
Scenario: A System Architect is creating a new Ruleset to store reusable UI elements for a 
division named "North America Finance". 
Question: According to Pega best practices, which of the following Ruleset names is valid? 
Options: 
Pega-NAFinanceUI 
NAFinance_UI 
NAFinanceUI 
NA Finance UI 
Explanation: Option 1 uses the restricted "Pega-" prefix. Option 2 uses an underscore (special 
character). Option 4 uses spaces. Only Option 3 follows all best practices.

Scenario 3: The Ruleset Stack Functionality 
Scenario: Two versions of an application are actively being used. The HR team is using v01-01 
of the app with the base UI, while a pilot group is testing v01-02 which contains a new SSN 

field. Both versions contain a Rule named "CollectEmployeeData". 
Question: What determines which version of the "CollectEmployeeData" rule is loaded for 
each specific user? 
Options: 
The Major version number 
The Application Layer 
The Ruleset Stack 
The Production Environment 
Explanation: The Ruleset stack is unique to each application version and dictates the exact 
sequence Pega searches to find and apply the correct version of a Rule.

Scenario 1: App Studio Background Generation 
Scenario: A citizen developer is building a case type in App Studio. They add a new "Collect 
Customer Information" View to an assignment step so the user can enter their name and 
address. 
Question: Which underlying Rule Type does Pega automatically create in the background to 
support this View? 
Options: 
Flow Rule 
Section Rule 
Data Page 
Action Rule 
Explanation: In Pega, a visual "View" built in App Studio directly translates to a "Section Rule" in 
Dev Studio, which controls the user interface rendering.

Scenario 2: The New Record Form 
Scenario: A System Architect is tasked with creating a highly customized routing algorithm 
that cannot be built in App Studio. They open Dev Studio to manually create a new rule. 
Question: When presented with the New Record form, which of the following combinations of 
information MUST the architect provide? 
Options: 
Rule Type, Ruleset, Apply to Class, Label 
Rule Type, Process, Section, Label 
Ruleset, Apply to Class, Label, Version 
.pzInsKey, Ruleset, Class, Rule Type 
Explanation: The core requirements to define the uniqueness and context of a new rule in Dev 
Studio are its Type, its naming (Label), its class scope (Apply to), and its storage container 

(Ruleset).

Scenario 3: Identifying Unique Rules 
Scenario: A Pega application has multiple Service Level Agreement (SLA) rules named 
"StandardApproval" across different classes. The system needs to uniquely identify the exact 
rule that was created on January 20th at 11:31 AM. 
Question: Which system property does Pega use to store the unique footprint of this specific 
rule? 
Options: 
.pyRuleName 
.pzInsKey 
.pxCreateDateTime 
.pyID 
Explanation: .pzInsKey is the ultimate unique identifier (Instance Key) for any rule in Pega. It 
concatenates the rule type, class, name, and timestamp.

Scenario 1: Identifying Class Types 
Scenario: You are building an application and need to configure a REST connector to fetch 
real-time weather data from a third-party web service. 
Question: In which class type should this connector rule be organized? 
Option 1: Work class 
Option 2: Data class 
Option 3: Integration class 
Option 4: Base class 
 
Explanation: The Integration class contains rules that describe how the application interacts 
with external systems.

Rule Search (Hierarchy) 
Scenario: An application has a rule named "CalculateTax". This rule exists in both the generic 
Organization class (TGB) and the highly specific Case Type class 
(TGB-Finance-Work-Expense). 
Question: When an Expense case is being processed at run time, which version of the 
"CalculateTax" rule does Pega select? 
Option 1: The rule in the TGB class. 
Option 2: The rule in the TGB-Finance-Work-Expense class. 
Option 3: It runs both rules sequentially. 
Option 4: It prompts the user to select the rule. 

Explanation: Pega always starts searching for a rule from the most-specific class in the 
hierarchy before moving to more general parent classes.

Scenario 3: Parent/Child Inheritance 
Scenario: You have a parent Case Type named "Onboarding" and a child Case Type named 
"ContractorOnboarding". The parent class has a standard UI rule called "CollectBasicInfo". 
Question: How does the "ContractorOnboarding" child case access the "CollectBasicInfo" 
rule? 
Option 1: The developer must copy and paste the rule into the child class. 
Option 2: The child class automatically inherits and can reuse the rule from the parent class. 
Option 3: A special Integration rule must be created to link them. 
Option 4: Child cases cannot use parent rules. 
Explanation: Class inheritance ensures that a child class can reuse any rules defined in its 
parent class without needing to duplicate them.

header: Scenario 4: Selecting the Right Layer for Reuse
content:
Scenario 4: Selecting the Right Layer for Reuse 
Scenario: A company named "GlobalCorp" has 5 different Pega applications (HR, IT, Finance, 
Legal, and Sales). They want to create a standard "Company Holidays" Data Rule that all 5 
applications can access and use. 
Question: In which class layer should the "Company Holidays" rule be created? 
Option 1: Application class 
Option 2: Work class 
Option 3: Organization class 
Option 4: Base class 
Explanation: The Organization class layer is specifically designed to hold rules (like data or 
integration) that need to be reused across all applications within the entire enterprise.

Scenario 1: Search Order Logic 
Scenario: A System Architect is troubleshooting a UI issue where the wrong "Customer Details" 
section rule is loading. The system is currently in the TGB-HR-Work-Onboarding class. There is 
a version of this rule in the TGB-HR-Work class (Pattern parent) and another version in the 
Work-Cover class (Directed parent). 
Question: Which inheritance path does Pega search first, and which rule will be applied? 
Option 1: Directed inheritance first; the rule in Work-Cover is applied. 
Option 2: Pattern inheritance first; the rule in TGB-HR-Work is applied. 
Option 3: Both are searched simultaneously. 
Option 4: It skips to the @baseclass. 
Explanation: Pega always searches the Pattern inheritance path first before falling back to the 
Directed inheritance path.

Scenario 2: Inheriting Pega Standard Rules 
Scenario: You are creating a new Case Type for processing employee travel expenses. You 
want this Case Type to automatically have access to standard Pega properties like 
.pxCreateOpName (which tracks who created the case) located in the standard Pega Work- 
class. 
Question: Which type of inheritance must be configured to access these standard Pega rules? 
Option 1: Pattern inheritance 
Option 2: Framework inheritance 
Option 3: Directed inheritance 
Option 4: Organizational inheritance 
Explanation: Directed inheritance is explicitly used to inherit standard Pega Platform rules and 
rules from outside your immediate business class hierarchy.

Scenario 3: The Ultimate Base Class 
Scenario: Pega is executing Rule Resolution to find a specific data transform. It has exhausted 
the Pattern inheritance path and the Directed inheritance path, following the chain all the way 
to the top of the class structure. 
Question: What is the final class Pega searches before returning an error, and from which class 
does it inherit? 
Option 1: Searches Work-; inherits from @baseclass 
Option 2: Searches @baseclass; inherits from None 
Option 3: Searches Pega-RULES; inherits from Work- 
Option 4: Searches @baseclass; inherits from Pega-RULES 
Explanation: @baseclass is the ultimate base class in Pega. It is the very last place Pega looks, 
and it inherits from absolutely nothing (None).

header: Scenario 1: Bridging Dev Studio and App Studio
content:
Scenario 1: Bridging Dev Studio and App Studio 
Scenario: A Senior System Architect creates a highly complex Service Level Agreement (SLA) 
in Dev Studio. A business architect working in App Studio wants to apply this SLA to a new 
assignment step but cannot find it in the drop-down list. 
Question: What must the Senior System Architect do to make the SLA visible to the business 
architect in App Studio? 
Option 1: Change the rule's class to the Organization layer. 
Option 2: Mark the SLA rule as a relevant record from the Actions menu. 
Option 3: Recreate the SLA directly in App Studio. 
Option 4: Save the SLA into a higher Ruleset version. 

Explanation: Rules created in Dev Studio are not automatically visible in App Studio prompts. 
They must be manually designated as relevant records.

Scenario 2: Automatic Promotion 
Scenario: A citizen developer uses App Studio to add three new data fields (First Name, Last 
Name, Email) to a Customer Information view. 
Question: What action must the developer take to ensure these new fields are available as 
relevant records for future reuse in other views? 
Option 1: Navigate to Dev Studio and manually mark them as relevant. 
Option 2: No action is required. 
Option 3: Add the fields to the Enterprise reuse library. 
Option 4: Check the "Reusable" checkbox in the App Studio settings. 
Explanation: When records like fields, views, or processes are created in App Studio, Pega 
Platform automatically marks them as relevant records.

Scenario 3: Deprecating Old Assets 
Scenario: Your application has a generic "Address" view that is marked as a relevant record. A 
new, more compliant "GlobalAddress" view has been created to replace it. You want to stop 
developers from seeing the old "Address" view in their App Studio drop-downs, but you cannot 
delete it because active cases still rely on it. 
Question: How do you achieve this? 
Option 1: Delete the rule and recover it if older cases crash. 
Option 2: Move the rule to a completely different Ruleset. 
Option 3: Mark the relevant record as inactive for that class. 
Option 4: Change the rule name to "DO_NOT_USE_Address". 
Explanation: Marking a relevant record as inactive removes it from the design-time selection 
prompts in App Studio without deleting the actual rule, ensuring existing runtime cases 
continue to function perfectly.

Scenario 1: Identifying Shapes by Color/Function 
Scenario: You are reviewing a Process diagram for an auto loan application. There is a step 
where the system must automatically generate and send an email to the applicant with their 
loan document. 
Question: What shape and color represents this automated email step in the Process Modeler? 
Option 1: Green Rectangle 
Option 2: Blue Rectangle 
Option 3: Yellow Rectangle 
Option 4: Orange Diamond 
Explanation: System automations (like sending an email or creating a case) are represented by 

yellow rectangles in a Pega Process diagram.

header: Scenario 2: Connector vs. Local Flow Action
content:
Scenario 2: Connector vs. Local Flow Action 
Scenario: During a "Review Application" assignment, an HR worker realizes the candidate's 
home address has a typo. The worker clicks a button to update the address on the current 
screen, saves it, and then continues reviewing the rest of the application without moving to the 
next step. 
Question: Which type of action did the HR worker perform to update the address? 
Option 1: Connector Action 
Option 2: Local Action 
Option 3: Subprocess Action 
Option 4: Decision Action 
Explanation: A Local Action allows a user to update information or perform a task at an 
assignment without advancing the Case to the next shape in the process.

Scenario 3: Branching with Business Logic 
Scenario: A company processes insurance claims. If a claim amount is under $500, it goes to 
an automated payment step. If it is $500 or more, it must route to a manager's worklist for 
manual review. 
Question: Which shape must you add to the Process diagram to model this conditional routing 
logic? 
Option 1: A blue subprocess shape 
Option 2: A green assignment shape 
Option 3: A yellow automation shape 
Option 4: An orange decision shape 
Explanation: Decision shapes (orange diamonds) are used to automate complex decisions and 
create conditional paths (branching) based on business logic.

Scenario 1: Choosing the Right Rule 
Scenario: An application needs to route an expense report. If the expense is less than $100, it 
goes to the Manager. If it is between $100 and $500, it goes to the Director. If it is over $500, it 
goes to the VP. 
Question: Which rule type is most appropriate to determine the correct routing destination? 
Option 1: When Rule 
Option 2: Decision Table 
Option 3: Process Flow 
Option 4: Data Page 
Explanation: Because there are multiple conditions and the expected result is a specific value 
(Manager, Director, VP) rather than a simple True/False, a Decision table is the correct choice.

Scenario 2: The Failsafe Mechanism 
Scenario: A Decision table calculates shipping fees based on Region and Weight. A new 
"Northwest" region was recently added to the system, but the developer forgot to add a row 
for it in the shipping Decision table. 
Question: What happens when an order from the Northwest region is processed through this 
Decision table? 
Option 1: The system throws a fatal error and stops processing. 
Option 2: The system returns a Null value. 
Option 3: The system loops back to the first row. 
Option 4: The system returns the result configured in the Otherwise row. 
Explanation: The Otherwise row acts as a catch-all. If no specific rows match the input data, the 
Decision table always returns the Otherwise result to ensure the process can continue without 
crashing.

Scenario 1: Business Agility & Maintenance 
Scenario: A company frequently updates the promotional discount codes in their order 
processing application. The marketing manager wants to be able to change these codes 
without submitting IT tickets and waiting for a new application patch. 
Question: How should the System Architect configure the system to meet this requirement? 
Option 1: Create a new Framework layer for the marketing manager. 
Option 2: Delegate the discount Decision table to the marketing manager. 
Option 3: Configure a Local Flow Action for the marketing manager. 
Option 4: Set the Decision table to evaluate all rows. 
Explanation: Delegation empowers Process owners (like the marketing manager) to update 
specific rules, such as decision tables, directly in the production environment to adapt to 
changing business conditions quickly.

Scenario 2: The Authority Matrix 
Scenario: A capital expenditure request must be approved by different levels of management 
depending on the amount and department. A $50,000 request might require approval from 
the immediate Manager, the Department Head, and the CFO. 
Question: How do you configure a Decision table to ensure all necessary approvers are added 
to the routing list instead of just the first one it finds? 
Option 1: Place the Decision table in a Subprocess. 
Option 2: Check the "Evaluate all rows" option on the Results tab. 
Option 3: Add an "Otherwise" row for the CFO. 
Option 4: Mark the Decision table as a relevant record. 
Explanation: Enabling the "Evaluate all rows" check box ensures that Pega evaluates every row 

in the table. If multiple rows evaluate to true, all corresponding actions (like adding multiple 
approvers to a matrix) are executed.

Scenario 3: Automated Assignment Routing 
Scenario: An application needs to assign incoming support tickets to different regional Work 
Queues (North, South, East, West) based on the customer's zip code. 
Question: Which Dev Studio feature allows you to automate this specific assignment routing 
based on multiple zip code conditions? 
Option 1: A Process Decision shape 
Option 2: A Decision table router 
Option 3: The Evaluate all rows setting 
Option 4: A delegated When rule 
Explanation: A Decision table router evaluates the logic (the zip code) and automatically 
determines the appropriate operator or Work Queue for an Assignment.

Scenario 1: Table vs. Tree Selection 
Scenario: You need to configure a routing rule for loan applications. The logic requires 
checking the applicant's credit score first. If the score is above 700, you then need to check 
their employment history. If the score is below 700, you need to check if they have a co-signer. 
Question: Which decision logic rule is best suited for this highly dependent, nested structure? 
Option 1: When Rule 
Option 2: Decision Table 
Option 3: Decision Tree 
Option 4: Process Modeler 
Explanation: When logic requires nested conditions (where the next question depends entirely 
on the answer to the previous question

header: Scenario 1: Choosing the Right Tool (Same Properties)
content:
Scenario 1: Choosing the Right Tool (Same Properties) 
​ Scenario: A company calculates annual employee bonuses based strictly on three 
factors: Job Level, Department, and Tenure (years at company). Every single employee 
is evaluated on these exact same three factors. 
​ Question: Which logic rule should the System Architect use to configure this 
automated decision? 
​ Option 1: Decision Tree 
​ Option 2: Decision Table 
​ Option 3: When Rule 

​ Option 4: Authority Matrix 
​ Explanation: Because the exact same set of properties is being evaluated for every case 
to determine an outcome, a Decision Table is the most efficient choice.

header: Scenario 2: The Consequence of Wrong Selection
content:
Scenario 2: The Consequence of Wrong Selection 
​ Scenario: A developer uses a Decision Tree to evaluate shipping costs based solely on 
"Weight" and "Destination Zone" for every package. 
​ Question: What is the negative consequence of using a Decision Tree instead of a 
Decision Table for this specific requirement? 
​ Option 1: The system will throw a routing error. 
​ Option 2: The configuration will result in many empty boxes. 
​ Option 3: The configuration will result in duplicate Conditions. 
​ Option 4: The Decision Tree will fail to return a value. 
​ Explanation: When you use a Decision Tree to evaluate the exact same properties, you 
are forced to recreate the same condition branches repeatedly for different value 
combinations, causing unnecessary duplication.

Scenario 3: Technical Limitations 
​ Scenario: You need to configure a purchase request approval process. If the request is 
over $10,000, it needs to be approved by the immediate Manager, the Finance Director, 
and the CFO. You need to dynamically build this list of approvers based on the amount. 
​ Question: Which automated decision rule MUST you use to support this cascading 
authority matrix? 
​ Option 1: Decision Tree 
​ Option 2: Process Subprocess 
​ Option 3: Decision Table 
​ Option 4: Delegated When Rule 
​ Explanation: In Pega, building an authority matrix for cascading approvals exclusively 
requires a Decision Table (using the "Evaluate all rows" feature). Decision trees do not 
support this specific configuration. 
Topic: Decision Rule Conflicts & Completeness 
​ Conflict tests: Identifies if a rule prevents one or more rows/branches from ever being 
evaluated (unreachable conditions due to top-down processing). 
​ Consistent Rule: A Decision rule that contains zero conflicts. 

​ Evaluate all rows Exception: If "Evaluate all rows" is enabled on a Decision table, 
conflict tests do not show warnings because all conditions are forced to evaluate. 
​ Completeness tests: Identifies missing conditions or unhandled branches (e.g., missing 
drop-down values or unhandled numerical boundaries) and suggests additional rows to 
ensure all scenarios are covered.

Scenario 1: Identifying a Conflict 
​ Scenario: A System Architect creates a Decision table for loan approvals. Row 1 checks 
if Credit Score > 600. Row 2 checks if Credit Score > 750. During testing, the 
architect notices that applicants with a score of 800 are receiving the Row 1 outcome 
instead of the Row 2 outcome. 
​ Question: Which testing tool in Pega would immediately identify why Row 2 is never 
being evaluated? 
​ Option 1: Show completeness 
​ Option 2: Show conflicts 
​ Option 3: Tracer tool 
​ Option 4: Rule delegation 
​ Explanation: "Show conflicts" identifies unreachable rows. Because 800 is greater than 
600, Row 1 evaluates to true first and stops the execution, meaning the > 750 
condition in Row 2 is completely unreachable.

header: Scenario 2: The Exception to the Rule
content:
Scenario 2: The Exception to the Rule 
​ Scenario: You have a Decision table with intentionally overlapping numerical conditions 
that would normally cause a conflict. However, when you save the form, the system 
does NOT display any conflict warnings. 
​ Question: What configuration setting suppresses these conflict warnings in a Decision 
table? 
​ Option 1: The table is marked as a Relevant Record. 
​ Option 2: The "Show completeness" button was clicked first. 
​ Option 3: The "Evaluate all rows" check box is selected. 
​ Option 4: The Otherwise row is left blank. 

​ Explanation: When "Evaluate all rows" is checked, Pega forces the evaluation of every 
single row regardless of previous true results, meaning no row is "unreachable," so 
conflict warnings are not generated.

header: Scenario 3: Ensuring All Scenarios are Handled
content:
Scenario 3: Ensuring All Scenarios are Handled 
​ Scenario: A developer builds a Decision tree to route customer service requests based 
on the "Request Category" property. The property is a local list with four values: Billing, 
Technical, Sales, and General. The developer only configures branches for Billing and 
Technical. 
​ Question: Which feature should the developer use to prompt the system to suggest 
adding the missing Sales and General branches? 
​ Option 1: Show conflicts 
​ Option 2: Show completeness 
​ Option 3: Pattern inheritance 
​ Option 4: App Studio background generation 
​ Explanation: "Show completeness" analyzes the property being tested and automatically 
suggests adding rows or branches for any values (like Sales and General) that have not 
been explicitly handled in the logic.

Scenario 1: Default Stage Behavior 
​ Scenario: A developer adds a new "Manager Review" Stage to a Purchase Order case 
type but forgets to configure any start or skip conditions for it in the properties panel. 
​ Question: What will happen when a case reaches this point in the life cycle? 
​ Option 1: The case will throw a routing error. 
​ Option 2: The Stage will automatically skip because no condition was defined. 
​ Option 3: The Stage will execute normally because Stages never skip by default. 
​ Option 4: The system will pause and ask the user if they want to run the Stage. 
​ Explanation: By default, a Stage never skips. If no conditional logic is applied, the Case 
will enter and execute the Stage normally.

Scenario 2: Skipping a Process 
​ Scenario: In an Auto Insurance claim, the "Vehicle Inspection" Process is configured to 
start. However, if the DamageType is equal to "Glass Only", the insurance company 
does not require an inspection. 
​ Question: How do you configure the Case Life Cycle to skip the inspection for 

glass-only claims? 
​ Option 1: Add a condition to the Process to skip when DamageType = "Glass 
Only". 
​ Option 2: Change the default behavior of the Stage to "Always Skip". 
​ Option 3: Create a Decision Tree inside the Process to end it immediately. 
​ Option 4: Mark the Process as an optional action instead. 
​ Explanation: Because Processes always start by default, you must configure a specific 
condition directly on the Process to tell the system to skip it when the data matches 
your exception (Glass Only).

Scenario 3: Combining Conditions 
​ Scenario: A "Background Check" Process should only run if the applicant is applying for 
a "Security" role AND their Clearance Level is less than 3. 
​ Question: How is this logic structured in Pega? 
​ Option 1: You must create two separate Processes. 
​ Option 2: You build a single condition using multiple fields and comparators linked by an 
AND operator. 
​ Option 3: You must use a Dev Studio Decision Table. 
​ Option 4: You place one condition on the Stage and the other on the Process. 
​ Explanation: You can easily build complex logic by stacking multiple conditions (Field + 
Comparator + Value) together using AND/OR logic directly in the Process configuration.

Scenario 1: Action vs. Process 
​ Scenario: You are configuring a travel booking application. Customers should be able to 
log in and modify their in-progress flight reservations at any time before the trip. 
Modifying a flight requires the customer to select a new date, confirm the new price, 
and submit payment details. 
​ Question: How should you configure this requirement in Pega? 
​ Option 1: Add a Case-wide Optional User Action. 
​ Option 2: Add a Stage-only Optional User Action. 
​ Option 3: Add an Optional Process. 
​ Option 4: Configure a local flow action on the current assignment. 
​ Explanation: Because modifying a reservation requires a series of multiple steps (date 
selection, price confirmation, payment), it must be configured as an Optional Process 

rather than a single-screen Optional User Action.

Scenario 2: Determining the Scope 
​ Scenario: In a mortgage application, an underwriter needs the ability to request a 
secondary credit check if they suspect fraudulent activity. This secondary check is only 
relevant while the case is in the "Underwriting" phase. It should not be available during 
the "Intake" or "Closing" phases. 
​ Question: How do you implement this requirement? 
​ Option 1: Configure a Case-wide Optional Action and use a When rule to hide it. 
​ Option 2: Configure a Stage-only Optional Action in the Underwriting Stage. 
​ Option 3: Add an Alternate Stage to the Case Life Cycle. 
​ Option 4: Configure a Skip Process condition on the Underwriting Stage. 
​ Explanation: When an optional task is only relevant during a specific portion of the 
case's lifecycle, it should be configured as a Stage-only Optional Action to ensure it is 
only accessible when appropriate.

Scenario 3: Promoted Actions Limitation 
​ Scenario: A System Architect wants to make the multi-step "Cancel Policy" optional 
Process highly visible to customer service representatives by displaying it as a button on 
the Case summary panel instead of hiding it in the Actions menu. 
​ Question: Why is the Architect unable to configure this? 
​ Option 1: The "Cancel Policy" must be Case-wide to be promoted. 
​ Option 2: Only Case managers can see promoted actions. 
​ Option 3: Pega Platform only supports promoting Optional User Actions, not Optional 
Processes. 
​ Option 4: The Actions menu must be disabled first. 
​ Explanation: Pega has a strict limitation: only single-step Optional User Actions can be 
promoted to the Case page as buttons. Optional Processes are not supported for 
promotion.

Scenario 1: Bridging the Business-IT Gap 
​ Scenario: A company is struggling because the business team's requirements are 
frequently misunderstood by the IT development team, leading to long delays and 
software that doesn't meet business needs. 
​ Question: How does Pega's low-code approach primarily solve this issue? 
​ Option 1: By requiring business users to learn Java. 
​ Option 2: By providing a common visual language that both stakeholders and 
developers can understand. 
​ Option 3: By removing the need for a development team entirely. 
​ Option 4: By automating the creation of business requirements documents. 
​ Explanation: Low-code platforms replace text-heavy code with visual models, creating a 
shared language that allows stakeholders to focus on business logic rather than 
technical implementation.

Scenario 2: Omnichannel Delivery 
​ Scenario: A bank wants to launch a new loan application process. They want customers 
to be able to apply via their website, their mobile app, and through a virtual chatbot 
assistant. 
​ Question: How does Pega Platform support this requirement efficiently? 
​ Option 1: By requiring the development team to write three separate applications. 
​ Option 2: By using omnichannel development features to build the logic once and 
deploy it across all required channels. 
​ Option 3: By only supporting web-based channels by default. 
​ Option 4: By purchasing a separate third-party integration for the chatbot. 
​ Explanation: Pega allows developers to unify their activities. You define the data and 
process rules once, and the platform can render the application across multiple 
channels simultaneously.

Scenario 3: Developer Productivity 
​ Scenario: A team of highly experienced Senior System Architects is hesitant to adopt a 
low-code platform because they believe it is only meant for non-technical "citizen 
developers" building simple apps. 
​ Question: Which statement best describes the value of low-code for professional 

developers? 
​ Option 1: Low-code platforms restrict professional developers from building complex 
logic. 
​ Option 2: Professional developers are not allowed to use Pega's low-code tools. 
​ Option 3: Low-code tools allow professional developers to build and extend robust 
applications more rapidly by streamlining everyday development tasks. 
​ Option 4: Low-code completely eliminates the need for professional developers. 
​ Explanation: Low-code increases productivity for everyone. It frees up professional 
developers from writing repetitive boilerplate code, allowing them to focus their 
expertise on solving complex, custom business problems.

Scenario 1: Best Practice for Development 
​ Scenario: A System Architect needs to create a new data object and configure a basic 
user interface for capturing customer addresses. The architect has access to both App 
Studio and Dev Studio. 
​ Question: According to Pega best practices, in which studio should the System 
Architect perform these tasks? 
​ Option 1: Dev Studio, because it provides more control. 
​ Option 2: App Studio, because it handles behind-the-scenes configuration and reduces 
errors. 
​ Option 3: Admin Studio, because creating data objects is an administrative task. 
​ Option 4: Either studio, as there is no preferred best practice. 
​ Explanation: Pega best practices dictate that even advanced technical team members 
should work in App Studio whenever possible to minimize programming errors and 
speed up development.

Scenario 2: System Monitoring 
​ Scenario: An application has gone live, and users are reporting that the system is 
running slowly during peak hours. The IT team needs to monitor system resources, 
check runtime information, and debug active processes. 
​ Question: Which studio provides the specific tools required for this technical staff? 
​ Option 1: Admin Studio 
​ Option 2: App Studio 
​ Option 3: Dev Studio 
​ Option 4: Prediction Studio 

​ Explanation: Admin Studio is the dedicated software administration space managed by 
IT staff for monitoring, debugging, and managing runtime system resources.

Scenario 3: Using Artificial Intelligence 
​ Scenario: A company wants to use machine learning to analyze customer emails and 
automatically predict whether the customer is happy or frustrated, routing the case 
accordingly. 
​ Question: In which studio would a data scientist build this text analytics model? 
​ Option 1: Dev Studio 
​ Option 2: App Studio 
​ Option 3: Admin Studio 
​ Option 4: Prediction Studio 
​ Explanation: Prediction Studio is specifically designed for data scientists to build, train, 
and manage machine-learning, predictive, and text analytics models.
